title: Hearing resumes after homicide ruling in case of man who died in custody: [FINAL C Edition]
article: A public hearing resumes today to determine whether a Vancouver police officer used unjustified force in arresting home- invasion suspect Jeffrey Michael Berg, who died in October 2000 while in police custody.
Last month, a coroner's jury ruled Berg's death a homicide, a neutral term that does not attach blame, but indicates that one person was killed by another.

This latest hearing, undertaken by B.C.'s Police Complaint Commissioner, is a quasi-judicial proceeding that will determine whether Const. David Bruce-Thomas abused his authority by using excessive force during Berg's arrest.

"This is a fault-finding procedure," Julie Berg, the sister of the deceased man, told reporters Monday following a case-management session held in preparation for today's resumption of the public hearing she initiated.
"It'll be much more volatile than the inquest. The use of force is what caused his \[my brother's\] death, in my opinion."

Commission counsel Dana Urban said Monday the adjudicator, retired provincial court judge Brian Weddell, will hear evidence to determine under a civil -- rather than criminal -- burden of proof if Bruce-Thomas abused his authority by using unnecessary force.
If he finds it has been proven, Weddell is empowered to reprimand, suspend, or -- as a maximum -- dismiss Bruce-Thomas from the police force.
The hearing, under the B.C. Police Act, began in April, but was adjourned pending the outcome of a coroner's inquest into Berg's death.
An autopsy showed Berg, 37, died from a blow to the neck that caused an aneurysm that led to a fatal heart attack.

Bruce-Thomas, who was responding to a 911 call in east Vancouver, admitted kicking Berg several times because the suspect resisted arrest. But the officer testified he couldn't recall how the deceased ended up on the pavement.
Urban told Weddell Monday that the term "causing the death" should not be included in the allegations against Bruce-Thomas.
"Whether you're satisfied that that force caused Jeff Berg's death is up to you," Urban told Weddell.
Julie Berg's lawyer, Cameron Ward, asked the adjudicator to ask the provincial government to pay for her legal counsel to ensure "a fair process."
Weddell declined, saying he "had no authority" to provide or request such funding.

Julie Berg said in a later interview she has been granted "limited standing," meaning she cannot participate fully in the proceedings and must request the right to question or cross-examine witnesses on a witness-by-witness basis.
She is, however, entitled to make a submission at the end of the hearing.
In more than a year of seeking answers surrounding her brother's death, the woman said she has run up legal bills -- still unpaid -- exceeding $150,000.
"It's been financially and emotionally draining," Berg said.
A freelance fashion designer, she questioned whether this hearing will be fair when she can't afford to retain a lawyer throughout the process.
"There are two sets of laws," Berg said. "There is one law for the wealthy and the rich, and there's another one for the regular citizen."
However, she said she hopes for a finding of fault that could lead to a possible civil lawsuit or criminal charges against Bruce- Thomas down the road.
About 33 witnesses -- including many of those who testified at the inquest will be called during the public hearing, expected to last three weeks.
